newsitem.title: UK: UK health spending should be better targeted - BMA.
newsitem.headline: UK health spending should be better targeted - BMA.

text.p: The limited resources of Britain's National Health Service should be allocated according to evidence that certain clinical procedures actually work, Dr. Sandy Macara, chairman of the British Medical Association, told the group's annual meeting in Edinburgh on Monday.
But he added doctors must beware that evidence of best practice is not being used to cut costs rather than to provide the best quality care.

Speaking just two days before the Labour government discloses its first budget, Macara emphasised the importance of providing adequate overall financial support for the health service. "The inescapable fact is that the NHS (National Health Service) is underfunded, both absolutely and relative to any comparable system elsewhere," Macara said, adding that a year ago the doctors' group had estimated the health system needed a cash injection of one billion pounds per year for five years, or an increase of about 15 percent in the budget.
Macara said the BMA welcomed the government's promised review of health funding but warned against "the introduction of new charges."

Prime Minister Tony Blair told Parliament earlier this month that Labour's review of NHS funding would aim to "...get the best value for money" but he declined to say whether or not the government was contemplating charges for certain patient services, such as prescription charges for pensioners and charges for non-essential hospital services.
Macara said the Private Finance Initiative, a programme to raise private capital for public sector projects, should not be allowed to "dictate patterns of care or to compromise clinical services."

Labour is currently reviewing the initiative, a programme started by the former Conservative government. Minister of State for Health Alan Milburn said earlier this month that money raised from the private sector would not be used for the provision of clinical services. Priority would be given to the construction of acute care facilities such as intensive care units.
